claims.text: The solid-to-liquid transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by temperature-induced surface compositional segregation.
Cu preferentially diffuses toward and becomes enriched at the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Surface Cu enrichment creates localized premelting.
Localized surface premelting subsequently propagates into the particle core.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are fully solid.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous.
Mild pre-annealing can be used to promote or suppress surface segregation.
An inert-gas environment minimizes oxidation as an extrinsic influence on the transition.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituents of the FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
High-temperature atomic diffusion drives Cu surface segregation.
Cu segregation produces a locally disordered or liquid-like surface region.
The liquid-like surface region lowers the effective melting-onset temperature.
Melting progresses from the particle exterior toward the core.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will melt at a lower onset temperature than untreated homogeneous nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface segregation will produce a distinct solid-liquid coexistence regime.
Initial premelting will be confined to surface regions and will be observable by diffraction and TEM.
Untreated homogeneous nanoparticles are expected to melt at a temperature predicted by bulk thermodynamics in the absence of prior surface-segregation effects.
The magnitude of the melting-onset shift may depend on particle size and subtle compositional variation.
The controlled comparison is between confirmed Cu-enriched pre-annealed particles and untreated particles heated under otherwise identical inert conditions.
Failure of confirmed surface-segregated particles to show either a significant onset-temperature reduction or a liquid-like surface region would falsify the hypothesis.
